What homestead exemption means in Connecticut

In Connecticut law, a homestead exemption shields a home from creditors. It is not a discount on the property tax bill. The rule is in section 52-352b of the General Statutes, and it limits what a judgment creditor can reach in a home.

Plenty of people search the phrase hoping to cut a tax bill, but the term means something else here. Tax relief for older, disabled, blind or veteran owners comes from other statutes with other names, covered further down.

How much of a home is protected from creditors

The statute protects the homestead of the exemptioner up to a value of $250,000. Value is the fair market value of the real property less any statutory or consensual lien on it. A smaller limit of $75,000 applies to money judgments that arise from a claim of sexual abuse or exploitation of a minor, sexual assault or other wilful, wanton or reckless misconduct by a natural person.

The number used to be far smaller. A 1993 law (Public Act 93-301) started it at $75,000, a 2003 act added $125,000 for hospital services judgments, and Public Act 21-161 swapped both for $250,000. The larger exemption applies in bankruptcy and postjudgment proceedings begun on or after October 1, 2021, whenever the underlying debt arose.

  • Statute: Conn. Gen. Stat. 52-352b(21).
  • Protected value: $250,000, measured as fair market value minus liens.
  • Reduced amount: $75,000 for the misconduct judgments described above.

Dollar limits get amended, so have a Connecticut attorney confirm today's number.

What counts as a homestead

A homestead is owner-occupied real property, a co-op, or a mobile manufactured home used as a primary residence. That definition is in section 52-352a(5). Public Act 10-181 added co-ops and Public Act 94-55 added mobile manufactured homes.

  • Owner-occupied: a house you rent to someone else is not a homestead for this purpose.
  • Primary residence: a second home or a vacation property does not qualify.
  • Exemptioner: the person claiming the exemption must be a natural person, so a house held in an LLC is outside the definition.

An inherited house you do not live in is not your primary residence, so the shield may not reach it. An attorney can sort out facts like that.

Mortgages and foreclosure

The exemption does not stop a mortgage lender. A mortgage is a consensual lien, and the statute measures the exemption after subtracting liens. Courts have said a mortgage is outside the homestead exemption. One decision also upheld a waiver that the homeowner gave voluntarily with a lawyer's help.

One appellate ruling held that homestead rights attach to the proceeds once a foreclosure sale is confirmed and turned into cash. Another ruling found that a trial court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over a homestead claim meant to protect the proceeds of a voluntary sale from a judgment lien creditor.

So the exemption speaks to what an unsecured creditor can take. If the problem is a mortgage in default, the options are a loan modification, a sale, or a deal with the lender, and a cash sale can close faster than a listing. Talk with an attorney or a HUD-approved housing counselor before you sign anything.

Property tax breaks that work like a homestead exemption

Connecticut's property tax exemptions for owners are listed in section 12-81 of the General Statutes. Several are fixed-dollar reductions in assessed value, and the ones that most resemble a homestead exemption depend on who the owner is.

  • Blind residents: property to the amount of $3,000 under subdivision (17).
  • Wartime military service: property to the amount of $1,000 under subdivision (19).
  • Service members with disability ratings: property up to $3,500 under subdivision (20).

These carry filing rules in other sections, and there are limits when a person qualifies under more than one category. Your town assessor takes the application, so call that office for forms and deadlines. The circuit breaker credit also runs through the assessor.

Conveyance tax relief for distressed sellers

A tax relief program can change the conveyance tax at sale. The Department of Revenue Services lists an exemption from the state conveyance tax for the principal residence of a seller who is approved for property tax assistance under section 12-129b or 12-170aa for the current assessment year, or who was approved within the prior 15 months or less. That deed is not exempt from the municipal portion. An estate of a person who was approved for tax assistance cannot claim this exemption.

The same list covers other cases that come up in distressed sales.

  • A deed in lieu of foreclosure on the seller's principal residence.
  • A principal residence that sells for less than the mortgages and senior tax liens against it.
  • A principal residence with a pyrrhotite crumbling foundation, when an engineer has put the evaluation in writing and the owner gets no money from the Crumbling Foundations Assistance Fund. Only the first transfer after that written evaluation is exempt.

Conveyance tax when a house is sold

Under section 12-494 the state takes three-quarters of one percent of the price at the base rate, and the municipality takes another one-quarter of one percent. Nothing is owed on a deed with consideration under $2,000. The state rate is higher, one and one-quarter percent, for property that is not residential, except unimproved land. Other rates apply to certain residential estates, so read the statute or ask the town clerk about a high-value sale.

PieceBase rateWho receives it
State portion0.75 percentState General Fund, remitted by the town clerk
Municipal portion0.25 percentThe town's general revenue

Form OP-236 goes in from the seller side, either by the grantor, an attorney or an authorized agent, and payment is made at recording. Many towns take the return and payment online through myCTREC. Elsewhere, mail or hand the paper form to the town clerk with a check payable to the Commissioner of Revenue Services.

Revaluations and late tax interest

Towns have to revalue real property on a five-year cycle under section 12-62, following a state schedule for each revaluation zone that starts October 1, 2023. A revalued house can land on a number far from the old one.

Disagree with a new value? Take it to the town's board of assessment appeals. A person aggrieved by that board's action can apply to the Superior Court no later than two months after the notice of the action was mailed, under section 12-117a.

Late payments are costly. Whatever is delinquent accrues interest at 18 percent a year from the due date. Each installment has a two-dollar minimum charge, which a town may choose to waive. At closing the collector's balance plus interest is normally paid out of your proceeds, so get a payoff figure early.

Checklist before selling a home with debts

List every debt and every recorded claim on the house. A title search turns up mortgages and liens, and the town tax collector states the tax balance. Then work through these steps.

  1. Confirm whether you live in the house as your primary residence, because that decides whether the creditor shield can apply.
  2. Ask your assessor whether you qualify for any exemption or the circuit breaker credit before the next filing window.
  3. Request a payoff from each mortgage lender and from the tax collector.
  4. Check which conveyance tax exemption, if any, matches your sale, and note its code.
  5. Speak with a Connecticut attorney if a judgment creditor is involved, since an exemption claim in court has its own procedure.

A cash sale leaves these rules as they are. It changes the timeline and removes repairs and showings.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a property tax homestead exemption in Connecticut?

Connecticut's statutes use the word homestead for a creditor shield of $250,000 in section 52-352b(21). Property tax relief comes from named programs such as the circuit breaker credit and the exemptions in section 12-81. Ask your town assessor which one fits you.

Can a creditor force the sale of my Connecticut home?

A judgment creditor can pursue equity above the exempt amount, and a mortgage lender is not limited by the exemption at all. Equity under $250,000 in a primary residence is protected from ordinary judgment collection. A lawyer can say how a given debt is treated.

Do I have to live in the house for the exemption to count?

Yes. The statute defines a homestead as owner-occupied property used as a primary residence, so a rental or a second home does not qualify. A person who inherited a house and lives elsewhere should not assume the shield applies.

Who files the conveyance tax return when I sell?

The seller, or the seller's attorney or agent, completes Form OP-236. Take it to the town clerk when the deed is recorded, or file through myCTREC if your town accepts it, and pay any tax then.

Where do I apply for a military or blind exemption?

Apply with your town assessor. Section 12-81 sets the dollar amounts, and the assessor's office has the forms and the filing dates for your town.

What the Connecticut estate tax covers

Connecticut taxes the transfer of a dead person's estate, and the tax falls on the estate of anyone who was a state resident at death. The rules are in Chapter 217 of the General Statutes, mainly section 12-391.

For deaths on or after January 1, 2023, there is no tax up to the federal basic exclusion amount and a 12 percent rate on the part above it. The tax payable is capped at $15 million, and Connecticut gift taxes paid since 2016 reduce that cap.

The tax base is the Connecticut taxable estate. For recent deaths that is the federal gross estate less allowable deductions, plus Connecticut taxable gifts made since 2005 that are not already in the gross estate, plus any Connecticut gift tax paid on gifts made in the three years before death. The state deduction for estate taxes paid is disregarded.

Executors and other filers deal with the Department of Revenue Services. The Probate Court also receives estate tax returns and return information, and it can issue certain lien releases, covered below.

How the exemption has changed

The part of an estate that escapes Connecticut tax has grown sharply in recent years, and it now follows the federal figure.

Year of deathEstate not taxed up toRate on the excess
2011 to 2017$2,000,0007.2 percent at the first bracket, rising by bracket
2018$2,600,0007.2 percent at the first bracket
2019$3,600,0007.8 percent at the first bracket
2020$5,100,00010 percent at the first bracket
2021$7,100,00010.8 percent at the first bracket
2022$9,100,00011.6 percent at the first bracket
2023 and afterFederal basic exclusion amount12 percent flat

The date of death picks the schedule, not the date of the sale. If someone died in 2021, the heirs follow that year's schedule even when the house closes years later.

The estate tax lien and your sale

The estate tax is a lien in favor of Connecticut on the real property that was transferred. Under section 12-398(d), the lien runs from the due date until the tax is paid, with interest and costs.

The lien has limits. It is not valid against a lienor, mortgagee, judgment creditor or bona fide purchaser until notice of it is filed or recorded in the town clerk's office or wherever such liens are recorded. A recorded notice shows up in a title search and could hold up a sale.

The statute offers two tools for a clean closing:

  • A certificate that the tax on the transfer of the property has been paid. It can be recorded with the town clerk and is conclusive proof that the tax was paid and the lien discharged.
  • A certificate of release of lien on the decedent's interest in the real property. It can be recorded and is conclusive proof that the property is released from the lien.

An estate under the threshold owes no estate tax. The task then is to get paperwork showing that nothing is due.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Connecticut house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Getting a certificate of release of lien

In most cases the Probate Court issues it. The Commissioner of Revenue Services issues it when the return must be filed with the Department. A person is entitled to a release when the court or the Commissioner finds, on satisfactory evidence, that payment of the tax is adequately assured or that no tax is due.

The court that acts is the probate court for the district where the decedent lived at death. If the decedent lived out of state, it is the probate court for the district where the real estate or tangible property is located.

An heir or executor planning a sale can work through these questions in order:

  • Did the decedent live in Connecticut, or only own property here?
  • Is the Connecticut taxable estate under the threshold for the year of death?
  • Does a return have to be filed with the Department of Revenue Services, which would route the release through it?
  • Has the release been recorded in the land records of the town where the house stands?

The Commissioner can adopt regulations setting the evidence a court or the Department must see before it finds that payment is assured, so ask the probate clerk what that court expects in your case.

If the owner lived outside Connecticut

Connecticut can tax the Connecticut real estate of a nonresident who died. The state may tax all real property in Connecticut and tangible personal property with an actual situs here, applying the tax to a fraction of the estate based on the share located in the state.

A special rule covers houses held in an entity. For a nonresident, real property owned by a partnership, S corporation or single-member LLC is treated as personally owned by the decedent in proportion to their ownership if the entity did not carry on a profit business, the ownership was not for a valid business purpose, or the property was acquired without a bona fide sale for full consideration while the decedent kept an interest or power.

Residency is presumed. Section 12-391(h) says each decedent is presumed to have died a Connecticut resident, and the estate must prove nonresidency. A filer who believes the decedent was a nonresident may request a determination of domicile after the return is filed, but only once 270 days have gone by since the due date and within three years of it. The Commissioner then has 180 days to decide.

When the federal figure changes later

If the federal estate tax is changed or corrected after filing, the filer must send Connecticut an amended return within 90 days of the final determination. Section 12-398 sets that deadline, and an amended federal return also triggers a 90 day amended Connecticut filing.

If the Commissioner finds additional tax due, the estate gets a notice with the extra tax and interest at 1 percent per month or fraction of a month, counted from when the original tax was due. The estate has 30 days from the mailing date to pay in cash, check, draft or money order payable to the Commissioner of Revenue Services.

If the estate overpaid and got no federal credit for it, the State Treasurer pays the refund on order of the Comptroller. Heirs who plan to sell should consider holding back part of the sale proceeds before distributing, in case a change comes later.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Connecticut houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Who can see an estate tax return

Generally nobody outside the process. Section 12-398(c) bars a probate court from disclosing estate tax returns and return information to any person or state or municipal agency, with limited exceptions.

The court must give the returns on request to the Probate Court Administrator and the Commissioner of Revenue Services. It may also share them with an executor, administrator, trustee, grantee, donee, beneficiary, surviving joint owner or other interested party who shows the court a material interest affected by the return.

A buyer or title company will usually see a recorded certificate rather than the return itself. An heir may need to show the court why access is needed.

Estate tax and property tax are separate bills

The estate tax does not replace local property tax. An inherited house keeps generating property tax while the estate is open. Under section 12-146, an unpaid tax or installment becomes delinquent after the first day of the following month and carries interest at 18 percent a year.

That interest keeps running even after a judgment for the town, and each part of a month counts as a full month. A slow estate can watch a property tax balance grow while the estate tax and probate steps are worked out.

Before closing on an inherited Connecticut house, line up these items:

  • Proof from the Probate Court or the Department of Revenue Services on the estate tax lien.
  • A payoff from the town tax collector for any unpaid property tax and interest.
  • Any mortgage or other lien on the house.
  • Authority for the executor or administrator to sign the deed.

Before you list the house

Start with the lien paperwork, since that is the item most likely to hold up a closing. Confirm the year of death, work out whether the taxable estate is under the threshold for that year, and ask the probate clerk or the Department which office will issue the release in your case. Check the Department's current filing instructions for the due date and extension rules.

A buyer who pays cash and takes the house as is can often close faster, but the same paperwork is still needed. Allow time for the release to be recorded in the town land records before the closing date.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Does Connecticut have an estate tax?

Yes. Section 12-391 of the General Statutes taxes the transfer of the estate of a Connecticut resident, and of a nonresident's Connecticut real property.

What is the Connecticut estate tax rate?

For deaths on or after January 1, 2023, it is 12 percent on the part of the estate above the federal basic exclusion amount, with tax payable capped at $15 million.

Is the estate tax a lien on an inherited house?

Yes. Section 12-398(d) makes the tax a lien on the transferred real property until paid, but it is not valid against a mortgagee, judgment creditor or good-faith buyer until notice is recorded with the town clerk.

How do I get a lien release to sell an inherited house?

Ask for a certificate of release of lien. The Probate Court issues it in most cases, and the Commissioner of Revenue Services issues it when a return must be filed with the Department.

What if the estate owes more after a federal change?

The filer must send an amended return within 90 days. Additional tax carries interest at 1 percent per month and is due within 30 days of the notice.

Steps of a Connecticut eviction

A Connecticut eviction is called summary process. It runs from a written notice to quit, to a court complaint, to a judgment, and then to an execution carried out by a state marshal. Notice rules are in section 47a-23 of the General Statutes and complaint rules are in 47a-23a. Each step has its own clock, and those clocks decide how long a landlord waits before a house can be sold vacant.

StageRuleStatute
Rent lateNine days of grace before a landlord may terminate for nonpayment (four days for a one-week tenancy)47a-15a
Notice to quitWritten notice giving at least three days before the quit date, with the reason stated47a-23
ComplaintMay be returnable six days, inclusive, after service, and returned to court three days before the return day47a-23a
Use and occupancyCourt may order payments while the case is pending47a-26b
After judgmentExecution stayed five days, Sundays and holidays excluded47a-35

Reasons a landlord can give in a notice to quit

A landlord cannot simply ask a tenant to leave. The notice has to state the reason in the statutory language or words of similar import, and section 47a-23 limits the reasons to a list.

  • The lease or rental agreement ends by lapse of time or by an express term.
  • The tenant violates the lease or the landlord's rules.
  • Rent goes unpaid past the grace period for residential property.
  • The tenant violates the tenant duties in section 47a-11.
  • Nuisance or serious nuisance.
  • The occupant never had a right to be there, or the right has ended.
  • An employee living in employer-furnished housing fails to leave after the job ends.

For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, a notice based on nonpayment ends the rental agreement for the period in which it is delivered and turns the tenancy into a tenancy at sufferance. The notice can also carry a use and occupancy disclaimer. That tells the tenant any payment after the quit date is accepted for use and occupancy only, with all rights reserved.

What happens after the tenant is served

If the tenant does not leave by the quit date, a commissioner of the Superior Court may issue a writ, summons and complaint setting out the facts that support immediate possession. When the tenant appears in the case, the landlord can ask for payments while the case is pending. The court orders them without a hearing unless the tenant objects within five days of the motion.

Section 47a-26b sets the amount at the last agreed rent, or at fair rental value when there was no agreed rent. The tenant must deposit those payments with the court within ten days of the filing of the motion. If a housing authority or another agency pays part of the rent, depositing the tenant's share meets the requirement.

Venue is the court location where the defendant lives or where the rental sits, at the plaintiff's choice. The case moves in short steps on paper. A tenant who answers, asks for mediation or raises a defense can still stretch the real timeline well past the statutory minimum.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Connecticut house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How long a tenant has to leave after judgment

The tenant gets a five-day stay of execution. Sundays and legal holidays do not count toward the five days. Under section 47a-35, an appeal can be taken only within that window, and a timely appeal stays execution until the case is finally decided. The exceptions are a finding by the judge that the appeal was filed solely for delay, or a tenant who does not post the required bond.

After judgment, section 47a-42 says the defendant and any other occupant bound by the judgment must remove themselves and their possessions at once, unless a stay applies. If one does, they must go when it expires. The statute also covers the removal and sale of unclaimed possessions. Sections 47a-36 to 47a-41 cover other stays.

If you plan to sell, do not set a closing date that depends on the tenant leaving until the execution date is known.

Senior and disabled tenants in larger buildings

Section 47a-23c applies to a tenant who lives in a building or complex of five or more dwelling units, or in a mobile manufactured home park, and who is 62 or older or has a qualifying disability. It also covers some tenants whose spouse, sibling, parent, grandparent or child lives with them and meets those conditions. A landlord may bring summary process against such a tenant only for these grounds.

  1. Nonpayment of rent.
  2. Refusal to agree to a fair and equitable rent increase.
  3. Material noncompliance with section 47a-11 affecting health, safety or the condition of the premises.
  4. Voiding of the rental agreement, or material noncompliance with it.
  5. Material noncompliance with the landlord's lawful rules.
  6. Permanent removal of the unit from the housing market.
  7. The landlord's good-faith plan to use the unit as a principal residence.

The rent increase, removal from the market and principal residence grounds cannot be used during a lease term. Selling the building is not on the list, so a sale alone does not clear out a protected tenant.

Removing a tenant without court

Don't. Connecticut has separate rules for lockouts, found in chapter 833 of title 47a, which covers entry and detainer. The Judicial Branch landlord and tenant page links guides on lockouts, a police training manual that addresses lockouts and self-help evictions, and a how-to for representing yourself in an entry and detainer case.

Section 47a-16 also limits entry. A landlord may not enter a rented unit without the tenant's consent except in an emergency, as allowed by section 47a-16a, under a court order, or if the tenant has abandoned the unit. Entry is limited to reasonable times apart from emergencies.

An owner who wants to sell a rented house should use the notice and court process, or reach a written agreement with the tenant. A shortcut can turn a sale problem into a damages claim.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Connecticut houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How an eviction affects a sale

An open eviction case does not stop a sale, but it changes who is likely to buy and when the buyer gets the keys. Buyers using a mortgage usually want vacant possession at closing. A house with an unresolved case, or a tenant holding over, is harder for them.

Owners in this spot usually pick one of these paths.

  • Finish the eviction, then sell vacant.
  • Sell with the tenant in place to an investor who will take over the lease.
  • Negotiate a move-out date in writing and tie the closing to it.
  • Sell as-is to a buyer willing to handle the tenant after closing.

Whichever path you pick, the tenant's security deposit goes with the property. Section 47a-21 treats a transfer of the landlord's interest as an assignment of the deposits, and the seller has to hand the full amount, with interest, to the new owner. Our Connecticut landlord and tenant page covers that rule in more detail.

Where to find official help

The Judicial Branch law library publishes a landlord and tenant research page with forms, a landlord's guide to summary process and a tenant's guide to eviction. It also links EvictionHelpCT.org, which describes the state's Right to Counsel program for eligible tenants, and Housing Matters information on where to file.

The Department of Housing posts mandatory landlord and tenant notice forms, a model lease and a pre-occupancy walk-through checklist. The Office of Legislative Research has reports on the eviction process, including one on recent changes (2023-R-0220). Deadlines in these statutes get amended, so confirm the latest wording with a Connecticut attorney before you rely on one.

What to gather before you list a house with a tenant

A buyer or title company will ask for paper, and having it ready shortens the sale. Pull together the lease or rental agreement, the rent payment history, and any notice to quit with proof of how and when it was served. If a case has been filed, add the complaint, any motion for use and occupancy payments, and the judgment or stay order.

Write down the quit date and the execution date if you have one. A buyer will want to see exactly when possession is expected, because that date drives the closing. Hold the security deposit information too, since it transfers with the property and the buyer will ask where the money sits.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How many days notice does a Connecticut landlord have to give?

Section 47a-23 requires a notice to quit that gives at least three days before the quit date, and the reason must be stated. Other rules can add time, so check the grounds that apply to your lease.

Can a tenant stay while the eviction case is pending?

Usually yes, but the court can order payments for use and occupancy under section 47a-26b if the tenant appears. The deposit is due within ten days of the filing of the motion unless the tenant objects in time.

What is the stay of execution after an eviction judgment?

Execution is stayed for five days from judgment, and Sundays and legal holidays are excluded. Under section 47a-35, an appeal must be filed within those five days.

Can I sell my house while a tenant is being evicted?

Yes. You can sell while a case is open, but a buyer who needs possession may wait for the execution. A cash buyer can purchase the house as-is with the tenant or the case still in place.

Where do I find the official eviction forms?

The Connecticut Judicial Branch law library page for landlord and tenant law links the summary process guides and housing forms. A Connecticut attorney can confirm which forms apply.

Where to record a Connecticut quitclaim deed

A deed is recorded on the land records of the town where the land lies. Section 47-10 provides that no conveyance is effective to hold land against anyone but the grantor and the grantor's heirs unless it is recorded in that town's records.

The recording office is the town clerk. There are 169 municipalities and no county recorder, so a house in Hamden is recorded in Hamden even though the state also groups towns into historical counties and planning regions. If a parcel sits in more than one town, ask each clerk how to handle the deed.

Leaving a quitclaim unrecorded puts both sides at risk. The grantee may hold paper that fails to protect against a later buyer or lender, and the grantor may still appear as owner of record when a lien or tax bill arrives.

What a Connecticut deed must contain

Section 47-5 requires a conveyance of land to be in writing, signed and acknowledged by the grantor, and attested by two witnesses. A quitclaim follows the same formalities as any other deed.

  • Written and signed by the grantor, or by an agent whose power of attorney was itself executed, acknowledged and witnessed as the statute requires.
  • For a corporation, limited liability company or partnership, signed by a duly authorized person.
  • Acknowledged as the grantor's free act and deed.
  • Witnessed by two people who sign in their own hand.
  • Showing the grantee's current mailing address.

When an agent signs under a power of attorney, section 47-10 also requires that power of attorney to be recorded with the deed, unless it is already recorded in that town and the deed refers to it. Families using a power of attorney for a parent's house often miss that second step.

Recording fees

Section 7-34a sets the fee at ten dollars for the first page and five dollars for each additional page. A quitclaim deed is among the statutory-form documents that carry those same charges, provided the deed follows the form in section 47-36c and carries the title "statutory form" in its heading. Some add-ons can raise the bill.

SituationAdded charge
Deed lacks the grantee's current mailing address$5 on top of the regular fee
Names not printed or typed beneath signatures, witnesses and notary$1 on top of the regular fee
Document requiring data sent to the Office of Policy and Management under 10-261b$2 on top of the regular fee
Copy of a recorded document$1 per page; certifying a copy is $2

The conveyance tax discussed below can apply as well, so ask the clerk for a total before you mail anything.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Connecticut house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Tax on a quitclaim deed

It depends on the price. The conveyance tax in section 12-494 applies to a deed or other instrument that conveys real property when the consideration is $2,000 or more. The tax follows the consideration and ignores the name of the form, so a quitclaim with real money attached is taxed like any sale deed.

At the base rates, the state takes three-quarters of one percent and the municipality takes one-quarter of one percent. Residential value above $800,000 and non-residential use carry higher state rates. Under section 12-499, the town clerk remits the state portion to the Commissioner of Revenue Services and the municipal portion becomes general revenue of the town.

Quitclaim deeds that are exempt from conveyance tax

Section 12-498 lists several exempt transfers, and these come up most with family quitclaims.

  • Deeds between spouses.
  • Deeds where the consideration is under $2,000.
  • Transfers that change only the identity or form of ownership, with no change in beneficial ownership.
  • Deeds in lieu of foreclosure that transfer the transferor's principal residence.
  • Deeds securing a debt, and deeds releasing property held as security.
  • Deeds made under certain superior court decrees named in the statute.

An exemption leaves the deed's other costs in place and does not erase the property tax. It also doesn't tell you whether the transfer is a good idea. A gift or no-price deed inside the family can still raise questions about an existing mortgage and about the owner's own plans. Those are attorney questions.

Liens and title problems

A quitclaim does not fix them. A recorded tax levy, a mortgage or an unpaid municipal bill stays on the property until it is paid or released, and the grantee takes the house with whatever title issues it already has.

Property tax is billed against the parcel. Section 12-111 lets a person who took title after the assessment date appeal the assessment, which shows the system expects ownership to change hands while a year's bill is open. A new owner should learn about the October 1 assessment and any unpaid installments before closing on a quitclaim.

If the quitclaim comes out of a divorce, an estate or a dispute among heirs, the court file or probate record may control what the deed can say. A title company can search the land records and tell you what is open.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Connecticut houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a house you received by quitclaim

You can, provided the deed was properly signed, witnessed, acknowledged and recorded, and the title searches clean. The buyer's title company will look at how you took title, and a gap in recording or a missing power of attorney will show up right there.

Sellers who got a house this way tend to face the same issues: back taxes, repairs, a co-owner who has not signed, or heirs who disagree. Cash buyers who purchase as-is deal with these files regularly. Begin with a clean copy of the recorded deed and the current tax bill, which together show who owns the house and what is owed.

With a cash buyer, closing speed depends mostly on how fast the clerk's office returns the recorded deed and how soon payoff figures arrive. If you live far from the property, ask the title company how to arrange the signing so the acknowledgment and the two witnesses satisfy section 47-5.

Documents to have ready at closing

Three papers carry most of the weight: the recorded deed, the tax collector's payoff statement and any power of attorney that was used. Add the town clerk's recording information, any court or probate paperwork behind the transfer, and a current mailing address for the grantee.

Check each name against the others. A deed that spells a grantor's name one way while the land records show another is a common reason for delay, and fixing it can mean a corrective deed and another round of recording fees.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a quitclaim deed in Connecticut?

With the town clerk in the town where the property is located. Under section 47-10, recording in that town's land records is what protects the grantee against third parties.

How many witnesses does a Connecticut deed need?

Two. Section 47-5 requires the deed to be in writing, signed, acknowledged by the grantor and attested to by two witnesses, and to include the grantee's current mailing address.

What is the recording fee for a Connecticut quitclaim deed?

Ten dollars for the first page and five dollars for each additional page under section 7-34a, plus any add-on charges the statute lists, such as $5 when the grantee's mailing address is missing.

Do I pay conveyance tax on a quitclaim deed?

If the consideration is $2,000 or more and no exemption applies, yes. The base rate is 0.75 percent to the state and 0.25 percent to the municipality. Deeds between spouses are exempt.

Does a quitclaim deed remove a tax lien?

No. A deed moves ownership and does not discharge a lien or an unpaid tax. Ask the tax collector and a title company what is open before you sign.

Cash Home Buyers in Connecticut

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Connecticut Tax Sales sale

Who runs a tax sale in Connecticut

The municipal tax collector. Connecticut has 169 municipalities, each with its own collector, and the sale procedure in section 12-157 is written for that officer.

When the collector levies a tax warrant on real estate, the collector prepares a notice listing the taxpayer's name, a legal description or a citation to the land records, the street address, the amount due as of the last day of the prior month, and the date, time and place of the sale. The notice must also say that more taxes, interest and fees accrue after the stated date, so the figure shown is a floor.

Because each town runs its own sale, scheduling, bidder rules and auction practice vary. The statute lets the collector publish or announce rules for orderly conduct of the auction, and lets the town hire auctioneers and clerks.

Steps before a house reaches a tax sale

The usual path starts with an unpaid installment, then interest, then a written demand, and only later a levy. Each step has its own statutory trigger. Read the notice you receive for the actual date and place.

StageWhat the statute provides
Installment dueTown sets one, two or four payments; last due at least 45 days before fiscal year end (12-142)
DelinquentUnpaid after the first day of the following month; interest at 18 percent per year, $2 minimum (12-146)
DemandCollector makes or sends demand when tax is unpaid 30 days after the due date (12-155)
Levy and noticeWarrant levied on real estate; notices posted; sale scheduled (12-157)
SaleAuction run by the collector; written notice of amounts due posted at the sale (12-157(d))

Redeeming after a Connecticut tax sale

You have no more than six months after the sale date to redeem. If the property was abandoned, or meets other conditions set by a municipal ordinance, the period can drop to sixty days. Both rules are in section 12-157(f).

The collector must give notice within sixty days after the sale. That means publication in a daily newspaper circulating in the town, plus certified mail, return receipt requested, to the delinquent taxpayer and to each mortgagee, lienholder and other encumbrancer of record whose interest is affected. The notice states the sale date, the purchaser's name and address, the price paid and the date the redemption period ends.

It also warns what happens if no one redeems by then: titles, mortgages, liens, restraints on alienation and other encumbrances in the property are extinguished. The deed to the purchaser stays unrecorded with the town clerk for six months from the sale.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Connecticut house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Who else gets notice

Mortgage holders and other lienholders get the same notice as the owner, because their interests are at stake.

  • The delinquent taxpayer.
  • Each mortgagee of record whose interest is affected.
  • Each lienholder and other encumbrancer with a choate interest.
  • The public, through newspaper publication.

A tax sale is rarely a private matter. A large mortgage on a house with tax arrears can pull the lender in, and the title company will see the levy in the land records. If you inherited the house, ask the collector which address the notices went to so you know what was sent and when.

What the purchaser can do during redemption

The purchaser's rights are limited. Section 12-157(g) gives the purchaser or the municipality an insurable interest in the buildings and improvements during the redemption period, and either may insure them against fire and other physical loss.

Either one may also petition the superior court for a receiver or other equitable relief when there is imminent danger of damage or destruction to the buildings, or of injury to people or other property from conditions on the lot or neighboring lots. The purchaser or municipality is not liable, and does not forfeit its interest, solely because it holds the tax deed, for conditions or events during that period.

Ask the collector who bought at the sale and what was paid. The post-sale notice must state both, along with the date redemption ends, and a title company will want all three.

Selling before the tax sale or during redemption

Selling at either point is how many owners clear the debt. Before a sale, the buyer's money pays the arrears with interest and charges out of the proceeds. After a sale, redemption requires paying what the statute and collector require, and the closing has to fit inside the redemption window.

The closing statement is simple: the payoff, any mortgage balance, and the conveyance tax if it applies. Under section 12-494, the base rate is three-quarters of one percent to the state and one-quarter of one percent to the municipality on a price of $2,000 or more. Tax deeds are among the transfers section 12-498 lists as exempt, but a deed from you to a buyer is a different instrument.

Timing is the big variable. A cash buyer who takes the house as-is can often move quickly, but a payoff statement, a title search and a signing date still take days. Start well ahead of the sale or redemption deadline and get exact figures from the tax collector in writing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Connecticut houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Stopping a sale and what to ask the tax office

A sale notice warns that taxes, interest and fees keep accruing past the stated amount, so any payoff needs the collector's confirmation. Call the office.

You can also contest the underlying tax, within limits. An assessment appeal has a February 20 deadline under section 12-111, and a court application must come within two months of the board's mailed notice under section 12-117a. Neither halts a sale already scheduled, so use them for the next tax year and talk to the collector about this one.

When you call, write down the answers with the date and the name of the person who gave them.

  • How much is owed today, with interest and fees, and the per-day or per-month increase.
  • Whether a warrant has been levied and whether a sale date has been set.
  • Whether a sale has already happened and, if so, the last date you can redeem.
  • The office's written procedure for paying off the account.

A seller's order of operations

If a levy notice or a sale date has landed in your mailbox, work in this order. First, call the collector and get the full amount owed with interest and fees, because the number printed on the notice is only a floor. Second, find out whether a sale has already been held, since that decides whether you are racing a sale date or a redemption deadline.

Third, line up the title work. A title company needs the payoff statement, the names of any mortgagee or lienholder who will be paid ahead of you, and a copy of the deed you took title under. Fourth, decide how you will close: through a listing, which needs time for showings and a buyer's lender, or as an as-is cash sale, which skips repairs, showings and a loan approval and can be scheduled around the deadline. Whichever route you pick, put every date you are given into one place and check it against the notice.

Frequently asked questions

Who holds a tax sale in Connecticut?

The municipal tax collector. Each of the state's 169 municipalities runs its own collection and sale, following section 12-157.

How long is the redemption period after a Connecticut tax sale?

No more than six months after the sale, or sixty days if the property was abandoned or meets conditions set by a municipal ordinance.

What notice must I get after a tax sale?

Within sixty days of the sale, the collector must publish a notice and mail one by certified mail to the taxpayer and to each affected mortgagee and lienholder.

What happens if I do not redeem?

The notice states that titles, mortgages, liens and other encumbrances in the property are extinguished if redemption does not take place by the stated date.

Can I sell my house to stop a tax sale?

Yes. The arrears, interest and charges are paid from the sale proceeds. Ask the tax collector for a written payoff figure and share it with the title company.

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Connecticut Property Tax Guide sale

Selling a Connecticut House? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Connecticut?
We buy Connecticut houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Who bills property tax in Connecticut

Property tax here is a local matter: your town or city does the assessing and billing. Connecticut is divided into 169 municipalities, made up of 19 cities, 149 towns and a single borough. They sit inside eight historical counties and nine planning regions, but the tax is a municipal matter, so no county bill is coming.

Population runs from 785 in Union to 148,654 in Bridgeport, and the same statutes govern both. Staffing, payment options and office hours differ, so a call to your own town hall will tell you more than any statewide summary. Four offices matter to a seller.

  • Assessor: values the property and keeps the grand list.
  • Board of assessment appeals: hears appeals filed by the February deadline.
  • Tax collector: bills, collects, sends demands and handles delinquent accounts.
  • Town clerk: records your deed and takes the conveyance tax when the sale closes.

How a Connecticut home is assessed

Every municipality uses an October 1 assessment date and assesses property at 70 percent of its present true and actual value. Both rules come from section 12-62a of the General Statutes.

That 70 percent trips up many owners. The tax bill is built from the assessed figure, not the market value, so if you set your assessment next to an asking price without adjusting, the assessment will look too low. It isn't.

The October 1 date also controls timing. The value on that date is the one used for the bill, even if you sell the following spring. Whoever pays that bill later is working from the house as it stood that October, not on closing day.

How often Connecticut revalues property

Revaluation happens every five years. Under section 12-62, each town revalues no later than the October 1 that falls five years after an assessment date set by a schedule the Secretary of the Office of Policy and Management prescribes for each revaluation zone.

Between revaluations the assessor works from the same values and adjusts for new construction, demolition and corrections. Revaluation years are when whole neighborhoods see assessments jump or fall together. If you plan to list or sell to an investor the year after a revaluation, expect the new value on your next bill, and expect the buyer to ask about it.

Ask the assessor when the last revaluation took effect and when the next one is due.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Connecticut house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Deadline to appeal an assessment

An appeal to the board of assessment appeals must be filed in writing or by electronic mail on or before February 20 under section 12-111. It has to include the owner's name, a description of the property, the reason for the appeal, the owner's own estimate of value and a signature. A few details trip up sellers and heirs.

  • Someone who took title after the assessment date may file.
  • A lessee bound by a recorded lease to pay property taxes can file.
  • The board must send hearing notice no later than March 1, and at least seven calendar days before the hearing.
  • For commercial, industrial, utility or apartment property assessed over $1,000,000, the board may decline to hold a hearing and must say so by March 1.

The date does not bend. If you inherit a house in January and the notice sits in a drawer, February 20 still holds. Ask the assessor for the form early.

Taking an assessment dispute to court

You can, within a short window. Section 12-117a lets a person aggrieved by the board's action apply to the superior court for the judicial district no later than two months after the board mailed notice of its action. The application carries a citation to the town and is served like a civil summons.

An appellant whose appeal the board chose not to hear can go straight to superior court under the same section. For a typical single-family house, that path is rarely worth it. What matters to a seller is the clock: two months from the mailing date, not from the day you read the letter.

Weigh the likely tax savings against the cost and against how soon you plan to sell. A house closing in six months seldom justifies a multi-year fight, though the right to appeal can pass to the buyer in some cases. A local attorney can run the numbers.

Due dates and late penalties

Each municipality decides its own schedule. Section 12-142 lets the town's legislative body choose one payment, two semiannual installments or four quarterly installments, with the last due no later than 45 days before the end of the fiscal year. Your bill shows the exact dates.

Paying late costs real money. A delinquent tax bears interest at 18 percent per year under section 12-146, with a minimum charge of $2 per installment unless the town votes not to impose it. An installment goes delinquent after the first day of the next month.

StepRule
Payment scheduleOne, two or four installments, set by the town (12-142)
Interest on late tax18 percent per year, $2 minimum per installment (12-146)
Written demandCollector sends a demand if tax is unpaid 30 days after the due date (12-155)
Levy and saleCollector prepares notices and may sell the real estate (12-157)
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Connecticut houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

Any unpaid bill is settled out of your proceeds. Before the deed is recorded, the title company or buyer usually checks the balance with the tax collector. Ask the collector for a current figure with interest, because last month's number will come up short.

A seller who is behind has two realistic choices: clear the arrears at the closing table, or wait. Waiting adds interest and, in time, a demand and a levy. The demand comes first, sent by the collector under section 12-155 when a tax is unpaid 30 days after the due date. A levy and tax sale follow if the account stays open, as our page on Connecticut tax sales explains.

An as-is cash buyer can close around these problems, since the payoff is one line on the settlement statement and not a financing contingency. The offer will account for the arrears and will not ignore them.

Conveyance tax at sale

The conveyance tax applies to deeds with $2,000 or more in consideration. Section 12-494 gives the state 0.75 percent of the price and the municipality 0.25 percent. The state rate climbs for expensive homes and for non-residential property.

  • Residential value up to $800,000: state rate of 0.75 percent.
  • Residential value between $800,000 and $2,500,000: 1.25 percent applies to the amount over $800,000.
  • Residential, above $2,500,000: 2.25 percent on the part above $2,500,000.
  • Property used for something other than residential use, except unimproved land: 1.25 percent.

Who pays, buyer or seller, depends on the contract and local custom, so read the purchase agreement.

Transfers exempt from conveyance tax

Section 12-498 lists many exemptions, and a few reach ordinary owners. Deeds between spouses are exempt, as are tax deeds and deeds that secure a debt or release security for one. The list also takes in some deeds made under court decrees, plus a deed in lieu of foreclosure when it conveys the transferor's principal residence.

So are transfers that change only the form of ownership with no change in beneficial ownership. An ordinary sale to an investor fits none of these. Assume the tax applies unless the town clerk or an attorney tells you otherwise.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

First steps for a seller

Start with the current bill and the assessor's property record, then ask the tax collector what it would take to pay the account off. Next, check whether the February 20 appeal window is still open and whether your town is in a revaluation year.

Keep a copy of every notice. If a demand or a notice of levy arrives, treat the date on it as a hard deadline, because the redemption period after a tax sale is short.

Frequently asked questions

What percent of value does Connecticut assess for property tax?

Seventy percent. Section 12-62a requires municipalities to assess all property at 70 percent of present true and actual value as of October 1.

What is the deadline to appeal my Connecticut property assessment?

February 20. The appeal goes to your town's board of assessment appeals in writing or by email, and it must state the reason and your estimate of value.

Can I appeal to court after the board rules?

Yes, within two months of the date the board mailed notice of its action, by applying to the superior court for the judicial district where the town sits.

What interest do I owe on late Connecticut property tax?

Delinquent tax accrues at 18 percent a year. Each installment carries a $2 minimum charge, unless your town voted to drop it.

Can I sell a house with property tax unpaid?

Yes. Balance plus interest is typically taken from your proceeds at closing, so request a fresh payoff figure from the collector.
